lead: Our Church keeps today the feast of the See of St Peter at Antioch, in the third week of the Great Fast. The three readings together draw a portrait of the one who is given charge of God's people. In Genesis, Abraham stands before the Lord and pleads for a city that is not his own. In Hebrews, the believers are told to remember those who led them, and to hold on to the one Lord who does not change when leaders pass away. In Matthew, a slave is put in charge of a household to feed the others at the proper time, and must answer for how he did it. The key words are standing before God, remembering and feeding: this is the feast of a ministry, of which the chair is the sign.

set: The scene follows straight on from Mamre, where Abraham welcomed three visitors and heard the promise of a son (18:1–15). As the visitors leave, the Lord decides not to hide from Abraham what he is about to do. He has heard a great outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah, and he will go down to see (18:20–21). The word “outcry” is the cry of people who suffer wrong.

Abraham's nephew Lot lives in Sodom (13:12), but Abraham never mentions him. He pleads for the whole city, and his question is about God's own justice. May the righteous be swept away with the wicked? Then the question grows: may the few righteous save the many who are not?
str: v. 22: the men go on toward Sodom; Abraham stays before the Lord.
vv. 23–25: the bold question about justice.
vv. 26–32: six requests, from fifty down to forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty and ten; each is granted.
v. 33: the Lord goes his way; Abraham returns to his place.
¶ Abraham is the one who stops counting. The text never says that God refused him.
kw: A person who is in right relationship with God and neighbour. Later in Genesis the same word is used by the king of Gerar, in 20:4.
A title that reaches past Israel to the whole world. Abraham appeals to God against the fear that God might act unjustly, and in so doing he confesses who God is.
A rhyming pair in Hebrew, found also in Job 30:19 and 42:6. It names the creature's lowliness and mortality. Abraham's boldness never forgets it.
vv: while Abraham remained standing before the Lord.

Ancient Jewish scribal lists count this verse among places where the wording was changed out of reverence, so that it once said that the Lord remained standing before Abraham. Scholars discuss how far these lists are reliable as history, but the tradition itself shows how astonishing the scene seemed: God waits for the man to speak.
Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
This is prayer, not rebellion. Abraham holds God to what God has shown himself to be. Only someone who trusts God's justice can ask this.
Let me take it upon myself to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes.
Humility and courage appear in one sentence. The prayer of the Bible does not choose between them.
For the sake of ten I will not destroy it.
God's answer never falls short of the request. Abraham's prayer begins to show something that Jeremiah 5:1 and Isaiah 53 will carry further: a few, or even one, may stand for many.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham's heart is attuned to his Lord's compassion for men and that he dares to intercede for them with bold confidence (CCC 2571). Christian intercession is a sharing in the prayer of Jesus, “the one intercessor with the Father on behalf of all men” (CCC 2634). The Church reads the shrinking numbers in the light of the one righteous man, of whom Paul writes: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). On a feast of Peter this reading says what a shepherd does first of all: he stands before God for his people.

r.h: Remember your leaders; the Lord does not change
set: The letter does not name its author, and calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). It seems to be addressed to Christians who had grown tired under pressure. Chapter 13 gathers its closing practical advice.

The leaders in verse 7 seem to be people who have already died, since their “outcome” can now be looked at. The first generation is passing, and new teachings are going about (13:9). The writer's answer is the sentence in the middle: Jesus Christ does not pass.
str: v. 7: remember those who spoke the word of God, and imitate their faith.
vv. 8–9: Christ the same; do not be carried away by strange teachings.
vv. 10–14: an altar, the sacrifice outside the gate, and the city to come.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifices that remain: praise, doing good, and sharing.
kw: “Those who lead”, a plain word and not a title of rank, used three times in this chapter (13:7, 17, 24). Here their leading consists in speaking God's word and in a life worth copying.
The Greek Old Testament uses this phrase for an offering of thanksgiving, as in Psalm 50. Here it is offered “through him”, through Christ.
Translated “to share what you have” in verse 16. It is the word for fellowship and for what the first Christians held in common (Acts 2:42). Hebrews names it, too, as a sacrifice.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
The Church's memory of her leaders is not nostalgia. The point of remembering them is to do what they did: to believe.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Leaders die and teachings change, but the one they preached does not. Every ministry in the Church, Peter's included, lives only by serving him.
We have an altar

Scholars discuss whether the writer is thinking first of the Cross or of the Eucharist. The Letter's own argument centres on the sacrifice of Christ, and the Church, feeding on that sacrifice, has not been wrong to hear in this line the altar of her own worship.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.

The writer sees a sign in the bodies of the sin offerings burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). His aim is to draw tired Christians toward Christ, not to speak against Israel, whose Scriptures he is using to think with.
Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
Together with verse 16, this ties worship and generosity into one offering. In the Great Fast, prayer and giving to others belong together.
ch: The Catechism uses verse 15 when it lists the names of the Eucharist, among them “the sacrifice of praise” (CCC 1330). For the Church's understanding of leadership, the feast points to Antioch itself. It was from that Church that St Ignatius of Antioch was led away to martyrdom at Rome. In his letters he urged the Christians to stay united with their bishop, and he is the first we know of to use the phrase “the Catholic Church” (To the Smyrnaeans 8).

r.h: The slave put in charge of the household
set: These verses come near the end of the long discourse on the Mount of Olives (chapters 24–25). Jesus has just said that no one knows the day or the hour (24:36). Now he tells a series of parables about the time of waiting.

In Luke's version of the same saying, Peter is the one who asks, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for everyone?” (Luke 12:41). The answer there, as here, concerns someone given charge over others. This explains why the parable suits a feast of Peter, though it speaks to everyone with any responsibility for others: parents, teachers, employers and clergy.
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise slave?
vv. 46–47: the blessing on the one found at work.
vv. 48–49: the other way of using the time.
vv. 50–51: the unexpected return and the judgement.
kw: Phronimos is practical good sense, the wisdom of the bridesmaids with oil in the next chapter (25:2). Faithfulness and common sense are asked for together.
The food comes when it is needed. A good steward does not feed people when it suits him.
In Greek, originally a stage actor. The wicked slave plays at being a steward while he uses the position for himself.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
He remains a slave among slaves. He is not the owner of the house. Authority here is defined by the food it gives.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
Readiness for the Lord's return is not anxious watching of the sky. It means being found doing the work given to you.
and he begins to beat his fellow slaves, and eats and drinks with drunkards,
Two sins of those in charge are named: harshness to those under them, and self-indulgence at their expense.
He will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites,
A fierce image in the style of parable. It is not a description to be taken literally, but its weight is real: responsibility for others will be answered for.
ch: The Catechism says that the office given to the pastors of God's people is in the strict sense of the term a service (CCC 1551). St Augustine told his people: for you I am a bishop, with you I am a Christian; the first is a danger and the second a grace (Sermon 340, in substance). St Gregory the Great called himself “servant of the servants of God”, and the popes have kept the title. Peter himself was given the same charge three times: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

qa: What is the See of St Peter at Antioch, and was Peter really there?

The New Testament places Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2:11), the city where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26). Early writers such as Origen and Eusebius connect him with the beginnings of the Church there. The New Testament does not say what title he held or how long he stayed, and we should not claim to know more than that. A “see” or “throne” is the bishop's chair, the sign of his office of teaching. The feast honours Peter's ministry at Antioch; it is not in competition with his see at Rome. The Catechism teaches that the Pope, as Peter's successor, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful (CCC 882).

Genesis tells the story in human terms, as a bargaining, and it wants us to feel the boldness of it. But the Lord himself begins the conversation, by not hiding his plan from Abraham (18:17), and he never refuses. The story shows a God who wants to be asked, and who draws a human being into his own mercy. Prayer does not teach God to be merciful. It teaches us to want what he wants.
Why does it stop at ten?

The text does not explain it. Abraham simply stops asking, perhaps out of reverence. The next chapter shows that fewer than ten were found, yet “God remembered Abraham” and brought Lot out (19:29). Abraham's prayer did more than he knew.
rite: Our Syro-Malankara Church prays in the Antiochene, West Syriac tradition, and in full communion with the Bishop of Rome. This feast joins these two sides of our identity: the Apostle who taught at Antioch is the one whose ministry continues at Rome. Our sister Churches of the Syriac tradition also honour the Antiochene see, and today is a good day to pray for the unity of all who look to Peter's confession. The Panchangam also remembers Thomas Mar Dioscoros (1943) and the anniversary of the consecration of St Mary's Cathedral, Thiruvananthapuram (1965), so that the universal and the local are held together in one day's prayer.
study: Abraham prays for a city he does not belong to. For whom, outside my own circle, do I pray in this Fast?
Who spoke the word of God to me? What in their faith can I imitate this week?
Hebrews 13:15–16 joins praise and sharing as sacrifices. How do these two come together in the way I take part in the Holy Qurbono?
In what place am I “put in charge” of others? What is the food they need from me at the proper time?
